lesson.title: When Chromosomes Break, Duplicate, or Rearrange
lesson.summary: Chromosomal abnormalities are changes in the normal structure or number of chromosomes, ranging from small structural rearrangements like deletions and translocations to whole extra or missing chromosomes, and they can significantly disrupt development because they alter the dose of many genes at once.
lesson.body:
A normal diploid human somatic cell carries 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 homologous pairs, one member of each pair inherited from each parent, while gametes are haploid and carry only 23 unpaired chromosomes. Chromosomal abnormalities are deviations from this normal structure or count, and biologists sort them into two broad categories: structural abnormalities, where the chromosome itself is broken and rearranged, and numerical abnormalities, where a cell ends up with too many or too few whole chromosomes. This chapter focuses mainly on the structural category, while later chapters build on it to explain how numerical abnormalities arise.

Structural abnormalities happen when a chromosome breaks and is repaired incorrectly. A deletion removes a segment of a chromosome entirely, so any genes in that segment are lost from that chromosome. A well documented example in humans is cri du chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of part of the short arm of chromosome 5, which produces distinctive developmental effects including an infant cry that sounds high pitched and cat like, which is where the condition gets its name. A duplication is the opposite problem: a segment of a chromosome is copied and appears twice, giving extra doses of the genes in that region.

Two other structural changes rearrange DNA without necessarily adding or removing it. An inversion occurs when a chromosome segment breaks in two places, flips around, and reattaches backward, reversing the order of genes within that segment. A translocation occurs when a segment breaks off one chromosome and attaches to a different, non-homologous chromosome. A well known translocation in humans is the exchange of material between chromosomes 9 and 22, which fuses part of one gene to part of another and creates an abnormal fusion protein that drives chronic myelogenous leukemia. This rearranged chromosome 22 is often called the Philadelphia chromosome.

Why do these rearrangements matter so much biologically. It comes down to gene dosage and gene context. Cells are remarkably sensitive to having the correct number of copies of each gene, so a deletion or duplication that changes how many copies of a stretch of genes a cell has can throw off the careful balance of gene products the cell needs, even if every individual gene sequence is still perfectly normal. Inversions and translocations can also disrupt genes directly at the breakpoints, or move a gene next to different regulatory sequences that change when and how much it is expressed. Structural abnormalities set the stage for the numerical abnormalities discussed in the next two chapters, since the same broad principle, that chromosome number and structure matter enormously to development, applies to both.
